children.text: This is Latino USA, the radio journal of news and culture.

I'm Maria Hinojosa. This time on Latino USA, a musical special. Latino alternative music making inroads in English language media. I don't really look at it as rock in Español. I just look at it as is this a good song, is this good music, are they good performers? With a lot of our listeners, they're listening more for the melody and the beats and just overall, the quality of musicianship, it's amazing. Also the hard rock sounds of the Puerto Rican band Puya and the multifaceted David Byrne and his record label, Luaka Bop. I tend to go to record shops and buy vinyl without knowing what it was on it. I got lucky sometimes and ended up with some really nice records. So we put out compilations of some of my favorite stuff. I wanted to let people hear the music I was listening to. This and more on this edition of Latino USA.

For this week, this is news from Latino USA. I'm David Alvarez. President Bush's original plan to grant temporary legalization status to almost 4 million undocumented Mexican immigrants may be in jeopardy. Latino USA's Patricia Guadalupe has more from Washington. President Bush had wanted the Temporary Guest Worker program to be finalized in time for Mexican president Vicente Fox's visit to Washington this September, but the president has met growing opposition from his own party, while Democrats have joined Latino leaders demanding permanent legalization for all undocumented immigrants, regardless of nationality.

Lisa Navarrete from the National Council of La Raza says she is concerned that the measure now may not pass. There seems to be a backing off on the idea of providing a legalization program, and much more focused on a guest worker program. Not going forward with this is definitely going to be a major blow to the Latino community. Congress is set to take up the issue when it returns from its summer recess next month. For Latino USA, I'm Patricia Guadalupe in Washington.

A new bipartisan survey released in Los Angeles shows that a majority of American voters support legalizing undocumented immigrants. Latino USA's Mandalit del Barco reports. At first, the 1,000 voters surveyed by telephone were divided. 40% said they favor legalizing undocumented workers, 49% were opposed. But when Republican and Democratic pollsters asked about immigrants already working and paying taxes in this country, support climbed to 59% in favor, 34% against.

Maria Elena Durazo is the president of the Hotel and Restaurant Employees Union. She says the poll confirms what her union members have been saying. Americans believe that if you work hard, if you pay taxes, you deserve to have the same rights as others. Immigrant advocates hope the results from the random sample with a 3.1% margin of error will influence Washington lawmakers who are debating the legalization issue. For Latino USA, I'm Mandalit del Barco in Los Angeles.

More than 1,000 business leaders, government officials, and community activists came together recently for a summit on issues affecting the US-Mexico border. From Edinburgh, Texas, Latino USA's Alex Avila has more. The US-Mexico border summit opened with a business roundtable to examine seven years of NAFTA.

But recent disputes, such as Congress's refusal to allow Mexican trucks access to US highways, has left many trade leaders complaining they have done a poor job of selling the benefits of NAFTA to the entire country. Sam Vale is with the Border Trade Alliance. It's not about McAllen, it's not about Laredo, it's not about San Diego, it's about all of us in trade and commerce. And unless we can understand that lesson, we're not going to get what we need out of those people in Washington and Ottawa and in Mexico City.

Panelists agreed that the trade community could potentially comprise a voting bloc of 230 members of Congress, if such an alliance could mature politically. For Latino USA, I'm Alex Avila in Edinburgh, Texas. This is news from Latino USA. Black and Latino leaders in New York City are cobbling together a coalition to back mayoral candidate Fernando Ferrer, who is hoping to be the city's first Latino mayor.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: From New York City, Kaari Pitkin has more. Religious leaders, activists like Reverend Al Sharpton, and insider Democrats have started to throw their weight behind the Bronx borough president in his bid for mayor. Prominent Harlem-based Congressman Charles Rangel said he had to overcome doubts Ferrer could win. There are four men seeking the Democratic nod, including frontrunner Mark Green, who received the endorsement of the city's first African-American mayor, David Dinkins. City Council Member Philip Reed says he expects the coalition building will influence voters. He adds that African-American voters are not monolithic, and all the contenders have, to varying degrees, proven records on issues important to Blacks and Latinos.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: I think Freddy has been unabashed about pointing out that in the Black and Latino communities, our issues are really indistinguishable from one another. The Democratic primary is September 11, and because it's a crowded field, it's expected there will be a runoff. For Latino USA, I'm Kari Pitkin in New York.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: The fatal police shooting of a Guatemalan immigrant in a Seattle suburb is moving many Washington State Latinos to organize and speak out. Erik Derr reports from Seattle. The Bellevue Police Department called the Community meeting to discuss the shooting of 24-year-old Nelson Martinez Mendez.

The meeting followed a 5-mile protest March through the city that drew about 200 participants. Latinos comprise about 5% of Bellevue's total population. Onofre Contreras, director of the state's commission on Hispanic affairs, says the shooting has spurred a grassroots effort to become more organized. The Latino communities themselves feeling energized and saying, "we need to begin working together within our own communities and then begin linking up with other people throughout the state." A handful of Latino residents are already forming a new community action group. For Latino USA, I'm Erik Derr in Seattle. In Austin, Texas, I'm David Alvarez. You're listening to Latino USA. I know you want to dance.

I'm Maria Hinojosa. Latino alternative rock groups are apparently making an impression on mainstream music fans. The new compilation album Escena Alterlatina, which features songs from South of the border and from local Latino bands from around the country, is one example of that increasing interest. The CD is selling well in top markets, getting play on public radio stations, and holding strong on college radio charts and the Billboard Latin top 50 charts. From San Francisco, Raquel Maria Dillon reports.

Everybody's jumping on this bandwagon But we're from the old school. For record producer and publicist Josh Norrick, every American indie rocker should experience Latino alternative rock and be converted, just like he was. Norrick hand-picked the songs for his compilation album Escena Alterlatina, the future sound in Español. I wanted to demonstrate the diversity of Latin alternative music, whether it's a group like Delinquent Habits or Mariachi Hip Hop from East LA or Orishas from San Francisco, who, in my opinion, are almost like a Latino answer to faith no more. Red Hot Chili Peppers, and then we've got Julieta Venegas, who is, I mean, just the most brilliant songwriter. I feel like in any language right now.

tags.tag: East Los Angeles, California, United States

children.text: Marketing this music is a really tough thing, because it's too edgy for Latin pop radio or ranchera, and often because of the Spanish lyrics, Anglo radio is afraid of it too. We've been lucky. With Live 105 in San Francisco, they had actually been spinning Orishas before I even did this album.

Welcome boys and girls to the local lounge. 105.3 San Francisco. Live. Live. At San Francisco rock station Live 105, DJ No Name, A.K.A., Mike Nelson, makes a special effort to scout out up and coming Bay Area bands for his nightly show Local Lounge. So he discovered two bands, Los Mocosos and Orishas. Just listening to the quality of their songs and their musicianship and seeing them live, it's kind of weird because at my angle, I don't really look at it as rock in Español. I just look at it as is this a good song, is this good music? Are they good performers? With a lot of our listeners, they're listening more for the melody and the beats, and just overall, like, the quality of musicianship, it's amazing.

Producer Josh Norrick pitches Escena Alterlatina to stations like Live 105 with this fact, at least 20% of rock radio listeners in big cities across the US are Latinos. DJ No Name says he's just doing his job as a righteous DJ in a corporate rock world. He looks for good, innovative music, and he found it in this new brand of rock in Español. That's one of the assets that rock in Español has. Is they can mix a lot of different styles up, and they have a lot more to pull from and say, "maybe your average kind of American band where it's just bass, drums, guitar." They can throw timbales in there, and they just throw it all together, and it's strong.

Rockeros are hoping that music lovers like DJ Noname will be similarly open-minded to cross-genre innovation. One DJ they can count on for adventurous new music is KCRW'S Nic Harcourt. The records he spins on his show, "Morning Becomes Eclectic," shape the musical preferences of Los Angeles' tastemakers. He can make a name for a new or foreign artist. It's only a matter of time before some of these artists start to cross over and break through. Now, if that's this year or next year or in five years, I don't really know. And will they have to sing in English? Maybe. But it seems pretty clear to me that audiences in general are more open now than they were perhaps five years ago. And the other irony of all of this, of course, is that it is guys like Ricky Martin and Marc Anthony and Christina Aguilera who are opening the doors.

Josh Norrick is trying to circumvent the big Latin labels to get to college radio, public stations, and discriminating listeners. Happy Sanchez of the San Francisco band Los Mocosos says sometimes it's just as hard to get to Latino listeners. Seven years ago, when I started Aztlán Records, there was no independent record labels, no independent distribution, no independent anything. (SINGING) We don't want to hear about the rep that we've acquired All we want to do is set this party off And we ain't going to stop until this place is on fire So if

you can't take the heat, we suggest you step off We don't need no water (SPEAKING) I'd approach these small retail stores and try to get them to carry some of our product. And they were just like, what? They didn't even understand what was going on. I think they thought I was some kind of carpetbagger or something. And this is just like punk rock, but even cooler because nobody even knows about this. This is really underground. Who would know that you'd see a bunch of Latin guys stage-diving off the stage. Judging from the success of Escena Ultra Latina on college radio charts, Latino alternative rock is emerging from the underground and coming into its own. For Latino USA, I'm Raquel Maria Dillon in San Francisco.

When most people think of the music of the island of Puerto Rico, La Isla del Encanto or the Island of Enchantment, they don't necessarily think of heavy metal rock music. But that's exactly what the group Puya does. (SINGING) Go! Go! Go! Go! Go! Described as Puerto Rican hardcore meets salsa, Puya breaks all categories. (SINGING) This is the Puya coming straight to ya. This is the Puya coming straight to ya. This is the Puya coming straight to ya. This is the Puya coming straight to ya.

This energetic quartet has been making a name in heavy metal circles among Anglos and Latinos alike. Their debut album, Fundamental, won the Billboard Latin Music Award for rock fusion album of the year. Their new release is called Union. And to talk about this unique mix is Ramón Ortiz, guitarist and co-founder of Puya, who speaks with us from the Maritime Hall in San Francisco just hours before a concert. Bienvenido, Ramón. Thank you. So I've got to tell you, of course, when I flipped this on, I was like, what? You grew up listening to what that made you decide that you wanted to do very, very, very heavy metal?

I guess you could say that what you hear is the result of being raised in Puerto Rico in the '70s and '80s. 208 Ortiz, Ramon We were exposed to a whole spectrum of music as youngsters and as young musicians. It's not like there was a point where we stopped, and we were like, "okay, I'm going to play this. I think the sound of the group today has been a natural evolution since we got together as a band." Well, help me out here, Ramón. Because I grew up in the '70s and '80s, too. And as I listened to your music, I, in fact, commented to someone that in terms of the rock music that I like, I tend to be a little bit more traditional. Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, that kind of thing.

So where did the leap to the death metal sound come in? The band started out in Puerto Rico in '91, I believe. It was slightly different idea than what the band is now. It was an instrumental trio, and we were doing something that wasn't quite as hardcore as what we do now. It was more of a fusion of blues, rock, maybe a little bit of funk. Very experimental but kind of progressive, a concept that was new to what local rock in the island was, until '93. We thought that we should move on because Puerto Rico is only so big. You can only play so many places.

So we moved to Florida, to Fort Lauderdale. There, the scene that we jumped in there, it was very, very heavy, way heavier than what we were used to in Puerto Rico. It was mostly hardcore bands, punk bands, metal bands. And I think the band got influenced by that, even though we always kept the Puerto Rican roots of the sound. Well, I have to say that the first song on the CD that really got me revved up was the cut entitled "Numbed." And I liked it not only because it's got the more traditional sound, but playing with rhythms, but I really appreciated the lyrics. It sounds there's a lot of political themes in your music.

Well, I come with colors of it. Normally it's more like a social comment. And it doesn't point a finger directly to anybody specific. It's just more about the system, about the way it robotizes people. Talk to me about this song, "Pa'Ti Pa'Mi." What are you trying to communicate with the lyrics? It is your most overtly political piece.

Well, it's just a look at the situation of the Navy in Vieques, and we thought we could contribute something to the whole cause with that song. And you believe that what should happen in Vieques? The Navy should get out of there immediately. In the liner notes of your CD, what was also interesting to me was that you have all of these pictures on one side of you and your families and getting together and holding your newborns and really communicating family. So your kids listen to this music with you? My baby is too little, but she listens to all kinds of music I listen to. I know parents get scared of that stuff. But I can totally get into it because I'm a musician. Even though it might sound like total noise to a different generation person, like my father.

My father, I play that stuff to my father, and he's like, what? There's no melody there. What's that? And what do you tell him when he says there is no melody? You say, papá. Hey, that's the way it is. There's not supposed to be a melody there. It's a different kind of music. Thanks very much for speaking with us. We've been talking to Ramón Ortiz, guitarist and co-founder of the group Puya. Their latest CD is entitled Union, and it's released by MCA Records.

The Latin Grammy Awards are set to take place on September 11th in Los Angeles. And just like last year, the award ceremony is mired in controversy. They were first scheduled to take place in Miami, but when the city ruled to let Cuban anti-Castro protesters near the ceremony site, organizers decided to move it to Los Angeles. For commentator Antonio Mejías-Rentas, in spite of the controversy, this year's Latin Grammy Awards have something new to show. I've never been a big fan of the Grammy Awards, never really trusted their ability to recognize the best music. So I was less than enthusiastic when the Latin Grammys were announced a couple of years ago.

It seemed as if the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences wanted desperately to cash in on the Ricky Martinizing of American pop culture. It wasn't like there was a need for another awards show. The country's Latin music industry already congratulated itself at the Billboard Awards, the Premios Lo Nuestro, the Premios Ritmo Latino, among other ceremonies. Still, that shiny miniature gramophone goes a long way in prestige and record sales. And this year's nominees showcase an eclectic mix of styles and sounds that come close to truly reflecting the immense richness of Latin music worldwide. Topping the list, Colombian rocker Juanes, whose album Fíjate Bien features a progressive mix of folk and contemporary sounds. The catchy yet haunting title song is an allegory to the violence in Colombia, warning of the dangers of casually stepping on a mine.

And it's not just the rockeros that give these Grammys some overdue respectability. Because the Latin Grammys cover music produced in both Spanish and Portuguese, there's a wide range of nominees in various styles of Brazilian music and categories for tango, flamenco, sertaneja, and other lesser known genres. Even in the more popular, radio-friendly categories, there are a few jewels to be found, like the modern classic "The Paisano a Paisano" from Los Tigres Del Norte or the party-inspired Me Gusta Vivir de Noche" from Los Tucanes de Tijuana, both competing in the norteño front. Since most of the Latin Grammy Awards rate only a passing mention in the televised broadcast, it seems irrelevant where the ceremony is actually held. With all respect to the Cuban American community and its undeniable right to protest, perhaps the Grammys should have never been taken to Miami.

The Latin Grammys should take a cue from this year's nominees and hit the international road. Rather than Los Angeles, Miami, or even New York, the show should move to the other music centers of the hemisphere, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro. Even San Juan, Bogota, or La Havana should all get a shot at hosting the ceremony. I think the Latin Grammys would improve the further they're taken from Hollywood. Not only would they become a true global celebration, I'm sure the ceremony would feature much better dance numbers. Commentator Antonio Mejías-Rentas is the West Coast entertainment editor for Mira Magazine.

children.text: David Byrne reached international acclaim and fame in the early 1980s with the rock group Talking Heads, who helped pioneer New York City's punk scene. Talking Heads has since retired, but Scottish-born Byrne has continued working as a performer, musician, film director, actor, photographer, and record producer. (SINGING) Home is where I want to be Pick me up and turn me round I feel numb, born with a weak heart I guess I must be having fun.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: In 1989, Byrne started a record label called Luaka Bop and released a compilation of Brazilian classics. The label has since been a welcoming home for new, traditional, and little-known artists. In New York, all during the '80s, I could walk outside my house and walk a few blocks and hear some of the greatest Latin artists in the world playing in the local clubs. And then I could walk around the corner and go to a rock club. And I thought, this is really great. I loved it. But I didn't find that it was represented in the music I was hearing, that in other ways, the cultures were segregated. Well, I started to really enjoy the music, and so I really wanted to work with some of those musicians someday. It became an ambition of mine.

tags.tag: New York, New York, United States

children.text: In 1989, David Byrne released his first solo album, Rei Momo. It was the second release on Luaka Bop and featured, among others, Latino artists like Rubén Blades, Celia Cruz, and Willie Colón. It was his first strong Latino sound. He received praise and controversy for what seemed to be an out-of-bounds musical move into Latino territory. (SINGING) It was a pretty picture It almost made me cry He's got a big imagination It's better than real life He can be a macho man (SPEAKING)

Surprisingly, it got a better reception in South America and Latin America than it did in the United States. In the United States, the reaction from, say, the rock community, which is the community I came out of, was, what are you doing this for? You're not supposed to do this. You're not allowed to do this. You don't belong doing this. Whereas I think south of the border, there was more of a reaction like, yeah, and we can do this, too, as if this is what a lot of musicians in Mexico, Argentina, Brazil, other places, were doing. And they seemed to be pleased to see that I was trying to do the same kind of thing that they were doing.

Luaka Bop acts range from traditional Cuban musician Silvio Rodriguez to Venezuelan disco rockers Los Amigos Invisibles. It's all popular music. All the artists pretty much are dealing with some form of popular music, but they're twisting it in some way or working on the edges of the mainstream. And the idea is that we're going to drag the center out towards the edge rather than moving the edge in towards the center.
David Byrne's latest release, Look Into The Eyeball, reflects his many musical influences. On the song "Desconocido Soy," he sings in Spanish with NRU, frontman of the Mexican rock group Café Tacuba.

At 49, David Byrne continues to explore the world of art in unconventional ways. For example, he just published a book with a very unique approach. Well, it's a bilingual book. On one side, it's called The New Sins, and the other side, Los Nuevos Pecados. The book describes the new sins. So basically I'm proposing that many things that we think are good are actually not so good, and that hell is populated by a lot do-gooders, website designers and people who write public announcements. David Byrne is a producer, musician, artist, performer, writer, and entrepreneur. His new record, Look Into The Eyeball, is a Luaka Bop release. His new book, The New Sins, Los Pecados Nuevos, is published by McSweeney's. This report was produced by Andrea Valdez.

And for this week, this has been Latino USA, the radio journal of news and culture. Thanks for listening. Latino USA was produced this week by Alex Avila, Deepa Donde, Walter Morgan, and Angelica Luévano. The executive producer is Maria Martin.

Additional production support was provided by Shereen Meraji, Alicia Rascon, and Chris. Further information about Latino USA is available on the web at latinousa.org. Or you can call our listener comment line at 1-800-535-5533. Or email us at lusa@npr.org. This week's program is number 437. I'm Maria Hinojosa. Join us again next week for another edition of Latino USA. National Public Radio.
